facebook.long_form:
⛳ The Wyndham Championship is underway — and for dozens of PGA Tour pros, this week is the most important of their season.

The 2026 Wyndham Championship opened Thursday at Sedgefield Country Club in Greensboro, North Carolina. The $8.5 million event plays on the iconic Donald Ross par-70 design, measuring 7,127 yards. Cameron Young returns as defending champion, having won last year's event by six strokes. After finishing runner-up at The Open Championship (losing by just one to Ryan Fox), Young enters this week in strong form.

But the storyline that will define this week isn't about the champion. It's about the bubble.

This is the FINAL PGA Tour regular-season event before the FedExCup Playoffs. After Sunday, the top 70 players in the FedExCup points standings will advance to the FedEx St. Jude Championship in Memphis, August 12-16. Everyone else goes home. Their season — however long, however full of promise — ends at Sedgefield.

That pressure shapes the way players approach this event. Every birdie on the Donald Ross layout isn't just a birdie — it could be the shot that saves a season. Every bogey could be the one that pushes someone below the cutline. With winning scores on this par-70 typically reaching 20-under, the leaderboard compresses quickly and players need to go low early.

The Wyndham has a reputation for dramatic finishes — not because of the trophy, but because of what's at stake beyond it. This year will be no different.

💬 Who are you watching this week at Sedgefield? Does anyone catch Cameron Young?

x_posts.text:
Jon Rahm. 2024 LIV individual champion. 2025 LIV individual champion.

Can he make it three straight at Bedminster this week?

938 points. 219-point lead. $4M on the line.

The case for Rahm being the dominant force in LIV Golf gets stronger every event.

#LIVGolf #Rahm

facebook.long_form:
🏌️ Jon Rahm arrived at Trump National Golf Club in Bedminster, New Jersey, this week with a simple mission: close out the LIV Golf Individual Championship and make it three in a row.

The 2026 LIV Golf New York tournament opened Thursday, and Rahm enters with what looks like an insurmountable advantage in the Individual Championship standings. His Legion XIII captain leads with 938.44 points — a margin of 219.04 points over second-placed Bryson DeChambeau (719.40 points). Lucas Herbert sits third with 531.23 points after winning two of the last four LIV events.

For DeChambeau to keep the individual title race mathematically alive, he needs to outscore Rahm by at least 19.04 points this week. Given Rahm's consistency and the size of the lead, that's a tall order.

If Rahm wins — or even finishes in a strong position relative to DeChambeau — he could effectively clinch the LIV Individual Championship for a third consecutive year. He won the title in both 2024 and 2025. A third straight crown would cement his place as the defining competitive force of the LIV era.

The event plays for $20 million — $4 million to the individual winner plus $10 million to the winning team ($3 million to the team captain). Trump National Bedminster has been stretched to 7,651 yards since 2023, making it one of the longer tracks on the LIV circuit.

💬 Can anyone slow Rahm down? Or is the LIV Individual Championship already over?

---

stories.title: Shiho Kuwaki Wins the AIG Women's Open at Royal Lytham
stories.angle: Recap of the dramatic playoff finish on Aug 2; Kuwaki beats Henseleit in 2-hole playoff after Henseleit holes 40-foot birdie on 72nd hole to force overtime; Japan's first Women's Open winner since 2019; $1.5M from record $10M purse

x_posts.label: Post 3
x_posts.text:
Shiho Kuwaki wins the AIG Women's Open.

Esther Henseleit holed a 40-foot birdie on 72 to force a playoff.

Then Kuwaki won the 2-hole sudden-death at Royal Lytham.

Japan has a new major champion. $1.5M from a record $10M purse.

What a finish. 🏆

#AIG #WomensOpen #LPGA

facebook.long_form:
🏆 The 2026 AIG Women's British Open ended with one of the most dramatic finishes in major championship history — and a new champion to match.

Playing at Royal Lytham & St Annes in England, the 50th staging of the AIG Women's Open came down to a two-hole playoff between Shiho Kuwaki of Japan and Germany's Esther Henseleit. Both players finished 72 holes tied at 5-under par (279), setting up the overtime drama.

How they got there was remarkable in itself. Henseleit — who had been trailing heading into the final holes — drained a 40-foot birdie putt on the 72nd hole to force the tie. It was a shock that silenced the Royal Lytham gallery and sent Kuwaki, who had carded a final-round 70, into a playoff she hadn't been anticipating just minutes earlier.

But Kuwaki held her nerve. She won the two-hole sudden-death playoff to claim the title, the trophy, and $1,500,000 from a record $10 million total purse. Henseleit received $994,669 as runner-up.

The rest of the leaderboard told its own story. Ayaka Noh had led entering the final round but shot 74, finishing T3. World No. 1 Nelly Korda and world No. 2 Atthaya Thitikul both finished tied for fourth — a result that will fuel questions about who can challenge them in the major championship setting.

For Kuwaki, this was a life-changing moment — her first LPGA Tour victory was on the sport's grandest stage. For the AIG Women's Open in its 50th year, it was a fitting celebration of everything that makes golf's major championships unpredictable.

💬 What a finish. Where do you rank this among the most dramatic major playoffs you've seen?

---

stories.angle: Scheffler at No. 1 with 4,123 points across 17 events; committed to St. Jude Aug 12-16; skipped The Open; the story of whether his massive lead survives a playoff format that partially resets the field

The last time he won? January. He's had 5 runner-ups since.

Something bigger is building. The Playoffs start next week.

#PGATour #FedExCup #Scheffler

facebook.long_form:
🏌️ Scottie Scheffler enters the FedExCup Playoffs as the dominant leader — and the player everyone else will be chasing to the final putt.

The world No. 1 and PGA Tour's most prolific winner of recent years has accumulated 4,123 FedExCup points across 17 events in 2026, placing him far ahead of the field in the race for golf's most lucrative prize: a $25 million FedExCup championship payout.

Scheffler's season has been excellent but also oddly quiet on the winner's side. His last victory was the American Express in January — his 20th career PGA Tour win, completed at 27-under par by four strokes. Since then, he's added five runner-up finishes, including a memorable T2 at the 3M Open behind Min Woo Lee's historic 59, and a narrow defeat to Rory McIlroy at Augusta.

Despite the lack of another win, his FedExCup lead is substantial — a testament to consistent top-10 finishes week after week. He has committed to the FedEx St. Jude Championship in Memphis, where the Playoffs begin next week (August 12-16).

The question the Playoffs will answer: can Scheffler close out a season's worth of consistent excellence with a title run, or will someone — McIlroy, Schauffele, Morikawa — find the hot streak at exactly the right time?

💬 Is Scheffler the lock to win the FedExCup, or is this the year someone catches him?

---

stories.title: FedExCup Playoffs Preview — What Fans Need to Know
stories.angle: Format (top 70/50/30 at each event), schedule (St. Jude Aug 12-16, BMW Aug 20-23, Tour Championship Aug 27-30), $25M to champion, key contenders to watch alongside Scheffler

The FedExCup Playoffs start NEXT WEEK. Here's how it works:

Top 70 - St. Jude (Memphis, Aug 12)
Top 50 - BMW Championship (St. Louis, Aug 20)
Top 30 - Tour Championship (Atlanta, Aug 27)
Winner - $25 million

Scheffler leads. McIlroy hunts. The hunt is on.

#FedExCup #PGATour

facebook.long_form:
📅 The FedExCup Playoffs start next week — and if you're not familiar with how they work, here's your complete guide to what's coming.

The FedExCup Playoffs represent golf's version of a postseason: a three-event gauntlet that narrows the PGA Tour field from 70 players down to 30, with a $25 million prize waiting at the end for whoever emerges from the Tour Championship victorious.

**FedEx St. Jude Championship — August 12-16 | TPC Southwind, Memphis, TN**
The opening event. The top 70 players in the FedExCup standings compete. Anyone outside the top 70 after the Wyndham Championship this week misses the Playoffs entirely. TPC Southwind is a demanding West-Tennessee course that rewards accuracy and putting consistency.

**BMW Championship — August 20-23 | Bellerive Country Club, St. Louis, MO**
The field narrows to the top 50 from St. Jude. Bellerive, the historic 1992 and 2018 major venue, is the traditional proving ground of Playoffs contenders. This is where the real sorting happens.

**Tour Championship — August 27-30 | East Lake Golf Club, Atlanta, GA**
The final 30. East Lake uses a staggered starting-score format to reflect the points standings — so Scheffler, as No. 1, begins at a significant advantage. The player who accumulates the best overall score wins the $25 million.

The contenders beyond Scheffler: Rory McIlroy (four-time FedExCup champion), Xander Schauffele, Patrick Cantlay, Viktor Hovland, and Collin Morikawa are all considered capable of the kind of hot streak that can overturn a points lead at the Tour Championship.

The best golf of the year happens in August. It starts next week.

💬 Who do you think wins the FedExCup this year?

---
